subsection: 9. Religious affiliation, cultural identity, ecumenism and cultural responses to the Troubles

notes.h: Religion and identity in Northern Ireland
notes.b: In Northern Ireland, which was created in 1921, religion was never only about belief. It marked which community a person belonged to, and so which political future they wanted. This is why the Troubles, the conflict that began in 1968-69, cannot be understood without it.
points: Unionists, who wanted Northern Ireland to remain in the United Kingdom, were mostly Protestant, and nationalists, who wanted a united Ireland, were mostly Catholic. Religion and political allegiance therefore overlapped, though the boundary was never absolute.

Catholics made up about a third of the population, about 35 per cent in the 1961 census, and Protestants were the majority. The Presbyterian Church in Ireland was the largest Protestant church, with the Church of Ireland and the Methodist Church also significant.

Unionist identity combined Protestantism, loyalty to the British Crown and attachment to the Union with Great Britain. Historical memory reinforced it: Protestants looked back to the Reformation, which split Christianity into Catholic and Protestant churches, and to the Boyne of 1690 and the Derry events of 1688-89.

Nationalist identity combined Catholicism, Irish cultural heritage and support for a united Ireland. Many nationalists were not practising Catholics, so the overlap was one of identity and community, not of personal belief.

Cultural identity means a sense of belonging through shared religion, language, history and customs, and in Northern Ireland it was tied to political allegiance. Cultural traditions are the distinct heritage, customs and practices of the unionist and nationalist communities.

Separate schooling, separate social life and marriage patterns kept the communities apart, so many people had little regular contact across the divide. Denominational identity was passed on through baptism and schooling, which reinforced the divisions across generations.

Sectarianism, meaning hostility between the Catholic and Protestant communities, grew in this setting. Bigotry is obstinate intolerance of people with different beliefs or identities, and tolerance is the opposite: accepting that others hold different beliefs and identities.
notes.tip: Examiners reward showing the overlap of religion and politics with named examples, not a general description. Remember that the overlap was one of identity, not belief, because not every nationalist was a practising Catholic.

notes.h: The Orange Order and Protestant tradition
notes.b: The Orange Order was the largest Protestant fraternal organisation (a society of members bound by oath and ritual). Its parades became both a focus of unionist identity and a cause of conflict.
points: The Order was founded in 1795 after the Battle of the Diamond, near Loughgall in County Armagh, a clash between Protestant and Catholic groups. Its origins were therefore in rivalry between the two communities.

Its central public ritual is the parade on 12 July, the Twelfth, which marks the Battle of the Boyne of 1690. The Twelfth is a public holiday in Northern Ireland, so the tradition is part of the calendar of the whole province.
Bands and banners are part of the parades, and bonfires are lit on the eleventh night, 11 July. These displays gave Protestant tradition a strong public presence in local communities.
Membership was open to Protestants only, and the Order was organised in local lodges (branches) in communities across the province. This is why it reinforced the separation of the communities.

The Order was closely linked to the Ulster Unionist Party, because Orange delegates sat on the Ulster Unionist Council, the party's governing body. Many unionist politicians were also members, so religion and politics were joined at the top.
Parades through or near Catholic areas were a source of tension, because residents regarded them as a display of dominance. Marches were often restricted or rerouted to avoid confrontation.
The Black Preceptory and the Apprentice Boys of Derry are related Protestant institutions with their own parades.
notes.tip: Say only that the Order was Protestant-only; do not claim flat rules about Orangemen marrying Catholics or attending Catholic services. Use the Order as a named example of how religion and identity overlapped.

notes.h: Catholic tradition, the GAA and the Irish language
notes.b: Catholic and nationalist identity rested on the Church, Gaelic sport and the Irish language. Together they gave nationalists institutions of their own, parallel to the Protestant ones.
points: The Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA) was founded in 1884 and promoted Gaelic games as an expression of Irish identity. It is not the same body as the Gaelic League.

The GAA's Rule 21 banned members of the RUC (the Northern Ireland police) and the British army from membership, and it was removed in 2001. It was a grievance for unionists and a symbol of separateness for nationalists.
The Ancient Order of Hibernians was a Catholic fraternal body that paralleled the Orange Order in its social and political role.
The Irish language had a small but active community in Northern Ireland. In 1971 an Irish-medium primary school (one teaching through Irish) opened at Shaw's Road in Belfast.

Catholic churches and schools were central to community life in nationalist areas, and the Catholic Church was a major provider of education. Church, parish halls and GAA clubs were the main centres of social life, so the community lived largely within its own institutions.

Nationalists felt that the Stormont state, the government of Northern Ireland, did not respect Irish identity. One example is the Flags and Emblems (Display) Act of 1954, which restricted the display of the Irish tricolour.
notes.tip: Strong essays use the Orange Order, the GAA and the language together as expressions of identity, with a named detail for each, such as 1795, Rule 21 or Shaw's Road in 1971.

notes.b: Ecumenism is dialogue and cooperation between Christian churches. It gained momentum in the 1960s from a change within the Catholic Church and from local initiatives in Northern Ireland, and it became more urgent once the Troubles began.
points: The Second Vatican Council, held from 1962 to 1965, was a gathering of Catholic bishops that encouraged dialogue between the Catholic Church and other Christian churches. This opened the way for contact that had been rare before.

The Corrymeela Community was founded in 1965 at Ballycastle, County Antrim, as a centre for reconciliation. Its founder was Ray Davey, a Presbyterian minister who had been chaplain at Queen's University Belfast.

The Irish School of Ecumenics was founded in 1970 in Dublin by the Jesuit priest Michael Hurley to promote reconciliation and interchurch dialogue. Do not confuse it with Corrymeela, which was Presbyterian-led, in Ballycastle, and five years earlier.
In 1973 the leaders of the Catholic Church and the main Protestant churches held their first formal meeting, at Ballymascanlon, County Louth. It was an official meeting of church leaders.

In December 1974 a group of Protestant clergy met IRA leaders at Feakle, County Clare, and the IRA declared a ceasefire over Christmas into early 1975. Unlike Ballymascanlon this was unofficial, a clergy initiative to end violence.
Pope John Paul II appealed for an end to violence at Drogheda on 29 September 1979, begging the men of violence 'On my knees I beg you' to turn away from violence. He did not visit Northern Ireland.
Ecumenism was supported by moderate church leaders, but it met hostility from hardline Protestant and Catholic traditions.
notes.tip: Exams set opportunities against problems: name Vatican II, Corrymeela, the Irish School of Ecumenics, Ballymascanlon and Feakle, and keep their dates and founders apart. A reasoned verdict earns more than a list.

notes.b: Ecumenism built contacts between churches, but it ran into opposition inside both communities and into the violence of the Troubles. Its limits explain why it did not change the political division.
points: Hardline Protestant opposition was led by Ian Paisley and the Free Presbyterian Church. They portrayed ecumenism as a betrayal of the Protestant faith and the Reformation.
In June 1966 Paisley led a march against the Presbyterian General Assembly in Belfast, and he was jailed for three months. This shows how hostile the hardline reaction to church contacts could be.

Catholic and Protestant clergy and lay people who joined joint initiatives were sometimes criticised or denounced by their own congregations or hierarchies (church authorities), so taking part could carry a cost.
Mixed marriage and joint worship faced disapproval in both communities. This limited the practical impact of ecumenism, because the closest personal contacts were the ones discouraged.
The Catholic Church's mixed-marriage rules, the Ne Temere decree of 1908, required the children to be raised as Catholics. They caused resentment among Protestants until they were relaxed in 1970.
Violence and sectarian killing undermined trust between the churches, and clergy were themselves targets of attacks, which made cooperation harder to sustain.
Ecumenism succeeded in building contacts and dialogue, but it did not change the political division between unionists and nationalists. This is why it is usually judged a limited success.
notes.tip: Give the problems as a set: Paisley, violence, the mixed-marriage question and no political change. Use the June 1966 march against the General Assembly as your dated example of opposition.

notes.h: Key personality: Ian Paisley (part 2, religion and politics)
notes.b: Paisley was a preacher, a protest leader and a politician, and his religion drove his politics. His opposition to ecumenism and to the Catholic Church shaped the hardline unionist position of the 1970s and 1980s.
points: Ian Paisley was born in Armagh in 1926. He founded the Free Presbyterian Church in 1951 and was its moderator (leader), and he combined his ministry with a political career.
He won the Bannside seat at Stormont in April 1970 and the North Antrim seat at Westminster in June 1970. He founded the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) in 1971 and led it until 2008.

He opposed ecumenism and any dialogue with the Catholic Church, and he attacked the Papacy and the Catholic Church in public speeches. In June 1966 he led a march against the Presbyterian General Assembly.

He was elected to the European Parliament in 1979, topping the poll in Northern Ireland. In October 1988 he interrupted Pope John Paul II there, in Strasbourg, calling him the Antichrist, and was removed from the chamber.

As a participant he was the leader and preacher at the centre of events, and he opposed Sunningdale and the Anglo-Irish Agreement. His religious beliefs drove these political stands, and events in turn gave him a platform.
Contemporaries saw him as a powerful and divisive figure, admired by his supporters and condemned by his opponents for his rhetoric (his forceful, inflammatory style of speaking).

The sociologist Steve Bruce, in God Save Ulster! (1986), argued that evangelical Protestant belief was central to Paisley's politics. Historians note that his religious politics made ecumenism more difficult.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the Free Presbyterian Church (1951) with the DUP (1971), or Bannside (Stormont, April 1970) with North Antrim (Westminster, June 1970). For a personality question give dates, an achievement and a verdict on how far he changed events.

notes.b: Seamus Heaney was the leading poet of the Troubles. Writing from inside the Catholic community, he explored violence, identity and the inheritance of the past.
points: Heaney was born on 13 April 1939 at Mossbawn, near Castledawson in County Derry, the eldest of nine children of a Catholic farming family. He was educated at St Columb's College, Derry, and Queen's University Belfast.
His early collections were Death of a Naturalist (1966), Door into the Dark (1969) and Wintering Out (1972). Do not confuse these with North, which came in 1975.

North (1975) drew on P. V. Glob's The Bog People and on Iron Age bog bodies, preserved bodies found in peat, such as the victim in 'Punishment'. The bog body became a symbol of ritual killing, a way to reflect on violence in Northern Ireland.

He moved to Glanmore, County Wicklow, in the Republic in 1972, which is a different place from Mossbawn. He later taught at Harvard, was Oxford Professor of Poetry from 1989 to 1994, and won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1995.
Field Work (1979) and Station Island (1984) continued his engagement with violence, memory and the Catholic tradition. He was a director of Field Day, though not a founder.
Ciaran Carson criticised North in a 1975 review for mythologising violence and making it seem inevitable. Others praised the poems as a major contribution to literature.
In 'An Open Letter' (1983), a Field Day pamphlet, he objected to being included in a British poetry anthology, writing 'My passport's green'. This shows his sense of Irish identity.
Historians see his work as a key cultural response to the Troubles, giving expression to grief, guilt and the search for an identity beyond sectarianism.
notes.tip: For an Ordinary Level paragraph, give four or five correct, dated statements: born 1939 at Mossbawn, collections, North in 1975 and the Nobel Prize in 1995. For higher level, give the title and year of each work.

notes.h: Cultural responses: drama, poetry and the arts
notes.b: Writers, playwrights, musicians and artists responded to the Troubles in many forms. The Field Day Theatre Company was a leading cultural initiative, set up to give Irish identity a voice in the arts.
points: Field Day was founded in 1980 in Derry by the playwright Brian Friel and the actor Stephen Rea. Its directors included Seamus Heaney, Seamus Deane, Tom Paulin and David Hammond, and from 1983 it also published pamphlets.

Friel's play Translations was Field Day's first production, at the Guildhall in Derry in September 1980. Set in Donegal in the 1830s, it deals with the Ordnance Survey's English renaming of Irish placenames and the loss of the Irish language.
Other poets from Northern Ireland, including Derek Mahon, Michael Longley and John Montague, explored identity, landscape and violence in their work.

Novels, plays and songs also dealt with life in the Troubles: Bernard MacLaverty's Cal (1983), Brian Moore's Lies of Silence (1990), Frank McGuinness's Observe the Sons of Ulster Marching Towards the Somme (1985) and Stiff Little Fingers' 'Alternative Ulster' (1978).
Film and television were further outlets through which writers and filmmakers responded to the conflict.

Murals in Catholic and Protestant areas of Belfast and Derry became popular forms of political expression. An example is the gable end at Free Derry Corner in the Bogside, painted in 1969, which reads 'You are now entering Free Derry'.
Cultural production in both communities reflected a desire to express identity, but it also reinforced the sense of separate traditions, which is the other side of the achievement.
Edna Longley, a critic, argued that Field Day's emphasis on a shared Irish culture neglected the unionist tradition.
notes.tip: Strong answers quote the title and year of each work, and use 'divided societies are culturally productive' as the judgement. Remember that Heaney was a Field Day director, not a founder: Friel and Rea founded it.

notes.b: By the late 1980s the government accepted that the two communities needed to understand each other's cultural traditions. The Cultural Traditions Group was a small cultural-relations body, not a political settlement.
points: The Group was set up in 1988 by the government's Central Community Relations Unit. It later came within the Community Relations Council, which was formed in 1990.
Its aims were to recognise both the unionist and the nationalist traditions and to encourage the sharing of culture across the community divide, so that each side would understand the other better.
Its work centred on cultural events, education and shared activity across the community.
The Education Reform (Northern Ireland) Order of 1989 made Education for Mutual Understanding and Cultural Heritage cross-curricular themes in schools, meaning they ran through several subjects.

Critics on both sides questioned whether equal recognition of traditions could replace political agreement on the constitutional question, that is, whether Northern Ireland should stay in the United Kingdom or join a united Ireland.
notes.tip: Treat the Group as a cultural-relations body, not as something that delivered political agreement. Be ready to state the criticism: could equal recognition replace political agreement?

notes.b: Judgement questions reward weighing what ecumenism and culture achieved against what they could not do. Both opened dialogue and gave expression to the conflict, but neither changed the political divide.
points: Strength: ecumenism built dialogue between churches and clergy, through Corrymeela, Ballymascanlon and Feakle, which gave some moderates a voice during the Troubles.
Limit: hardline religious opposition, led by Paisley, together with violence, restricted ecumenism and made dialogue politically costly.
Strength: Heaney's poetry and the Field Day movement gave a language to the violence and to the search for identity.
Limit: cultural initiatives did not change the political divisions between the communities. Some critics also argued that they reached mainly educated and middle-class audiences.
Contemporary view: unionists saw religious and cultural traditions as central to their British identity and resisted anything that appeared to dilute them.
Contemporary view: nationalists saw their culture and religion as the basis of a distinct Irish identity, which they wanted recognised within a united Ireland.
Later view: historians argue that cultural responses to the Troubles were genuine and productive, but that they were not sufficient on their own to resolve the political conflict.
notes.tip: A reasoned verdict earns more than a list. Pair each success with its limit, and note that each community saw its own religion and culture as central to its identity.

keyTerms.definition: The distinct heritage, customs and practices of the unionist and nationalist communities in Northern Ireland, which the Cultural Traditions Group sought to recognise.
A person's sense of belonging to a community through shared language, religion, history and customs, which in Northern Ireland was closely tied to unionist or nationalist allegiance.
The movement for dialogue and cooperation between Christian churches, which in Northern Ireland included the Corrymeela Community and the Irish School of Ecumenics.
Obstinate intolerance of people with different beliefs or identities, which both sides in the Troubles were accused of showing.
Tolerance is willingness to accept differing beliefs and identities, while intolerance is refusal to accept them, a central divide in Northern Irish society.
The Protestant fraternal organisation founded in 1795 whose parades on 12 July became a focus of unionist identity.
The cultural company founded in Derry in 1980 by Brian Friel and Stephen Rea, which staged Translations and produced pamphlets on Irish identity.
The Christian reconciliation community founded in 1965 near Ballycastle, County Antrim, by the Presbyterian minister Ray Davey.
The party Ian Paisley founded in 1971 and led until 2008, opposed to power sharing with nationalists and to the Anglo-Irish Agreement.
The sporting body founded in 1884 to promote Gaelic games, central to nationalist cultural identity.
The institute founded in Dublin in 1970 by Michael Hurley to promote interchurch dialogue and reconciliation.
